entries.title: A Crack in the Barn
entries.body:
Mia was spending the summer at Grandma's farm, where every day was full of new adventures. But what took hold of Mia most was a little white egg, lying in a warm nest in the corner of the barn.

Grandma explained that a chick was hiding inside the egg and that it would hatch when it was ready. "Patience," she said with a smile. "Such things cannot be hurried." Every morning Mia ran into the barn and peeked into the nest, but the egg lay stubbornly still.

One morning it was different. A quiet knocking came from the egg, and then the shell cracked. A little beak poked through, and soon out peeped a small, yellow chick. It was wet and helpless, but full of life. Mia bent down and promised to take good care of it.

entries.title: The Light in the Storm
entries.body:
On a rocky cape by the sea stood an old lighthouse. In it lived a keeper named Jakob, who lit the great lamp every evening. Its light reached far out over the waves and showed the ships the way past the dangerous rocks.

One wild night a storm broke out like nothing Jakob had ever known. The wind howled, the rain beat against the windows, and the waves crashed against the rocks. In the middle of the darkness, Jakob suddenly saw a small fishing boat struggling with the waves. The people on board could not find the way to the harbour.

Jakob knew what he had to do. All night he stood by the light and made sure it did not go out. Whenever the flame flickered, he built it up again. He was tired and chilled to the bone, but he did not give up.

Toward morning the storm died down. The fishing boat sailed safely into the harbour. The people on board said that, without the lighthouse's light, they would have been lost in the dark night. Jakob smiled and, weary, went off to rest. His light had once again guided someone home.

entries.title: The Bird That Swims
entries.body:
A penguin is a bird that cannot fly. Its wings have turned into strong flippers, so it is a true master of swimming. Under the water it moves so fast and so smoothly that it looks as if it is flying — only it flies through the sea.

Most penguins live in the cold south, where everything is full of ice and snow. A thick layer of fat and dense, smooth feathers keep them warm. When it is really cold, penguins press together into a big huddle and warm one another.

On land they walk slowly and waddle from side to side. On the ice they often throw themselves onto their tummies and slide, which looks very funny. Parents care for their chicks together and keep them warm under their own warm tummies.

entries.title: The Narwhal’s Tusk
entries.body: A narwhal is a whale that lives in Arctic seas. The long tusk seen on many males is actually an enlarged tooth. It grows in a spiral and contains nerves that may sense changes in the water. Narwhals use clicks to explore dark water and locate prey beneath sea ice. They travel in groups and must find openings where they can rise to breathe. The tusk looks like a horn, but its origin is quite different: it is a tooth extending through the upper lip. It is most often seen in males, although there are exceptions. Under the water, sight alone is not enough to find food in darkness or cloudy conditions. A narwhal produces clicks and listens to the returning echoes. These sounds give information about the space ahead. At the surface, the animal faces another challenge. It breathes air, so ice must leave suitable openings along its route. A large body, a long tusk, and a cold ocean make an extraordinary picture, but the everyday tasks remain finding food, breathing, and travelling with other whales.

entries.title: Across the Serengeti
entries.body: The Serengeti is a region of grasslands and woodlands in East Africa. Large herds of wildebeest and zebra move in search of fresh grass and water. Protected areas in Tanzania and Kenya help conserve this movement and the habitats it depends on. A herd’s movement is not a parade with a fixed starting bell. Rain changes where grass grows, and the animals respond to food and water. The route crosses a landscape with rivers, open plains, and areas of woodland. Different animals use that landscape differently. A grazing zebra, an insect in the grass, and a bird searching the ground do not need exactly the same things.

entries.title: The Hidden City in the Clouds
entries.body:
High in the mountains of South America, among clouds and steep peaks, hides the ancient stone city of Machu Picchu. It lies in the country of Peru, on top of a steep mountain ledge, kilometres above the valley below.

The city was built more than five hundred years ago by the Inca, a people who once ruled a great part of South America. Out of large stones they built houses, stairways and terraces. They cut and fitted the stones so precisely that even today you cannot slide a sheet of paper between them — and all without any mortar to hold them together.

Then something strange happened. The people left the city, and for long centuries Machu Picchu lay hidden from the world, overgrown with forest and wrapped in mist. Only a little more than a hundred years ago was it found again, and the world was amazed at its beauty.

Today thousands of visitors climb the steep path up to Machu Picchu every year. When they step among the old walls, high above the clouds, they feel just how skilled and wise the builders of this mysterious city must have been.

entries.title: The Mountain That Spews Fire
entries.body: A volcano is a mountain that can spew out fire. Deep under the ground it is so hot that the rock melts into a thick, glowing liquid. This melted rock is called magma. It is so hot that it glows red and orange. Slowly it cools and hardens into hard black stone. That is why the slopes of many volcanoes are made of hardened lava.

entries.title: Why Food Has Flavour
entries.body: The tongue detects basic tastes such as sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and savoury. Much of flavour also comes from smell. While we chew, scent molecules travel from the mouth toward smell receptors in the nose. A blocked nose prevents many of those signals from arriving, so food may seem less interesting. Texture, temperature, colour, and past experiences also help the brain build the complete flavour we notice. Flavour is more than the signal coming from the tongue. Odour molecules can reach the nose from food in the mouth as well as from food held near it. The brain combines these messages with information about texture and temperature. A crunchy apple and smooth apple sauce can therefore feel quite different even when they share many ingredients.

entries.title: The Travelling Drop
entries.body: Water continually moves between land, oceans, and air. Sunlight warms liquid water and some becomes invisible water vapour. Higher in the air, cooling vapour forms tiny droplets that gather into clouds. Rain or snow returns water to the surface, where it may soak into soil or flow toward rivers. This water cycle reuses the same water while moving it through many places and forms. A drying puddle has not lost its water into nothing. Molecules have escaped into the air as water vapour. That vapour is invisible, unlike the tiny droplets or ice crystals that make up clouds. After rain falls, its path is not always a quick trip into a river. Some soaks into the ground, some is taken up by plants, and some remains in lakes or freezes. Water can spend very different lengths of time in these places. Drawing several arrows from a rain-soaked patch of ground is therefore more accurate than drawing only one. The cycle is a network of routes, powered in large part by sunlight and shaped by gravity and living things.

entries.title: Spinning Seeds
entries.body: Maple seeds have thin wings. When a seed falls, it spins like a tiny helicopter. The spinning slows its fall and gives the wind more time to carry it away. A seed that lands beyond the parent tree may find open light, water, and soil. In spring, a successful seed can sprout roots and begin growing a maple of its own. The seed’s journey begins with a change of direction: instead of dropping like a stone, it rotates through the air. Its wing is part of the fruit carrying the seed. Slowing the fall gives moving air more opportunity to carry it sideways. Landing farther from the parent may reduce competition for light and other resources, but travel alone does not guarantee success. A seed on a pavement has a different chance from one in suitable soil. If conditions allow germination, a root begins to develop and a shoot follows. The spinning shape is therefore only the transport stage. The next stage depends on moisture, temperature, and the place where that little traveller comes to rest.

entries.title: The Treehouse
entries.body:
All summer the old oak tree at the end of the garden had been waiting for something. Then Dad brought home a pile of wooden boards, and Leo, Ella and their cousin Ben knew exactly what to do.

Leo climbed up first with the hammer. Ella passed the boards up to him one by one, and Ben carried the longest planks from the pile. Their dog Biscuit did not carry anything, but he watched every nail with great interest. Building was harder than it looked. One board was too short, another was crooked, and a bag of nails fell into the grass.

By evening the little house had four walls, a window and a ladder. The three builders sat inside, and they listened to the leaves whisper around them. It was the best room in the world.

entries.title: The Little Silver Key
entries.body:
While digging in Grandma's herb garden, Noah's spade hit something hard. He brushed away the soil and found a little silver key, dark with age. It was far too small for any door in the house.

Grandma turned it over in her hand and smiled. “I know this key,” she said. “I lost it when I was about your age.” She fetched a wooden chest from the shed and set it on the garden table. The key turned with a click, and the lid creaked open.

Inside lay postcards from the mountains and the seaside, a bundle of letters, and an old photo of a little girl. “That was me,” Grandma laughed. They spent the whole afternoon reading the postcards one by one, while the cat watched from the herb pots. Noah had wanted to find treasure. He had found Grandma's stories instead.

entries.title: A Home for the Kitten
entries.body:
The rain had not stopped all day. Mia sat by the window and watched the drops run down the glass, when a thin sound came from the garden. It was not the rain. It was a tiny, frightened meow.

Under the hedge, Mia found a small grey kitten, so wet that its fur stuck to its body. It was shivering. Mia lifted it carefully and carried it inside under a jumper, out of the rain.

In the warm room Mia poured some milk into a bowl. At first the kitten only sniffed at it. Then it drank and drank, until the bowl was empty and its whiskers were white. Mia made a bed out of a basket and a soft blue blanket. The kitten climbed in, turned around twice and curled up into a ball.

Mum said a kitten needs a name. Mia thought for a long time and chose Raindrop, because of the day they had met. Outside the rain went on falling, but Raindrop was warm, full and fast asleep. From that evening on, the small grey kitten had a home.

entries.title: The Chest in the Cellar
entries.body:
Ella did not like the cellar. The air smelled of stone and dust, and the only light came from an old lantern. But Grandpa had asked her to fetch a jar of plum jam, so down she went.

Behind the jars, in the darkest corner, stood a wooden chest with iron corners and a big rusty lock. Ella had never noticed it before. A small key hung from a nail beside it. She tried it. The lock gave a tired click, and the heavy lid swung open.

There was no gold inside. There were old books with cracked leather covers, bundles of letters tied with string, and old brown photographs. One photo showed a man and a little girl in a white dress. On the back someone had written a date from long ago.

Ella forgot the jam. She sat down on the cold floor with the lantern beside her and read until Grandpa came looking for her. “Ah,” he said softly when he saw the photo. “That little girl is your great-grandmother.” Then he sat down beside her, and together they turned the pages.

entries.title: Hunting in the Dark
entries.body:
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Their wings are not made of feathers but of thin skin, stretched between very long fingers. By day, bats sleep hanging upside down in caves or hollow trees. When the sun goes down, they wake up and set off to hunt.

It is dark, but a bat does not need much light. As it flies, it sends out short, high calls. The sounds are so high that our ears cannot hear them. When a call hits a moth or a mosquito, an echo bounces back. From the echo the bat knows exactly where the insect is, how big it is and which way it is moving. Then it snaps it up in the air.

A small bat can catch hundreds of insects in a single night. Every one of them might have bitten you.

entries.title: The Smiling Axolotl
entries.body:
The axolotl is a salamander that lives in only one place in the wild: lakes and canals near Mexico City. Its wide mouth looks like a smile, and on each side of its head it wears a crown of feathery gills.

Most salamanders change as they grow up. They lose their gills, leave the water and live on land. The axolotl never does. It keeps its gills and its tail all its life and stays in the water, like a tadpole that never becomes a frog.

It has another amazing talent. If an axolotl loses a leg, it simply grows a new one. It can even repair parts of its heart and brain. In the wild axolotls are dark brown and very rare today. The pink ones, like the one in the picture, are bred by people and kept in aquariums.

entries.title: Seeing with Sound
entries.body:
Deep water is often dark and cloudy, and eyes are not much help there. Yet dolphins find fish with ease, even at night. Their secret is sound.

A dolphin sends out fast clicks from the front of its head. The clicks travel through the water, hit whatever lies ahead and bounce back as echoes. From these echoes the dolphin builds a picture of its surroundings: a rock, a sunken ship, a shoal of fish. It can tell how far away a fish is, how big it is and in which direction it is swimming. It is a little like seeing with your ears.

Dolphins also hunt as a team. A pod will circle a shoal of fish and drive it together into a tight ball, so that every dolphin can dart in and grab a meal.

Because a dolphin is a mammal, it breathes air. It comes up, blows out a puff of spray through the hole on top of its head, takes a quick breath and dives again. A dolphin can stay under for around ten minutes, but usually it comes up far sooner.

entries.title: The Largest Animal of All
entries.body:
The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, heavier than any dinosaur. A grown blue whale can be thirty metres long, longer than two buses in a row. Its heart is the size of a small car, and its tongue alone weighs as much as an elephant.

You might think such a giant eats giant food. In fact it eats some of the smallest creatures in the sea: krill, tiny shrimp-like animals no longer than your finger. The whale swims into a swarm of krill with its mouth wide open, takes in a huge gulp of water and pushes it out again through the comb-like plates in its mouth. The krill stay behind and are swallowed. In one day a blue whale can eat around four tonnes of them.

When it comes up to breathe, the whale blows a cloud of spray high into the air, as high as a house with three floors. People on whale-watching boats often see this spout long before they see the whale itself.

Blue whales sing too. Their deep, slow songs travel hundreds of kilometres through the ocean.
